raw_response:
I’m 58 now, and I still do it mostly the way we all do here: look at last year, look at the money in hand, and look at what the neighbors are doing. My land is only 10.1 mu, not much, so I can’t afford to gamble. Wheat and maize are my steady crops, because even if the price is not great, they are reliable and I know the timing well. Cotton can still bring some cash if the year goes smoothly, so I’ll keep a small piece in cotton, but not too much because it takes more labor and picking is troublesome when family members are away for off-farm work.

For wheat, I’ll do about the same as usual on the better part of the land. I’ll sow in early October, use the common local seed, and put most fertilizer at the start, then add some urea around jointing if the seedlings don’t look strong enough. Water is from the well, but pumping costs money, so I won’t irrigate too many times unless spring is especially dry. After wheat harvest in June, I have to move fast into maize. That turn is always tight, so I won’t do fancy tillage, just quick residue clearing and shallow preparation so I can sow maize right away. For cotton, I’ll keep a smaller area. Cotton can make money, but it needs more watching and more hand work, so at my age and with less family labor at home, I won’t expand it.
